title: Fermat's little theorem and Euler's theorem

runs.text: Let p be prime and let
count the residue classes modulo n that are coprime to n.
Fermat's little theorem is the prime-modulus case of Euler's theorem because
For a base coprime to n, exponents may be reduced modulo
. The smaller multiplicative order, when known, gives a sharper period.

items.text: Euler's theorem requires gcd(a,n)=1; do not reduce exponents by phi(n) when that hypothesis fails.
The form a^(p-1) congruent to 1 requires p not to divide a; the form a^p congruent to a does not.
These theorems give sufficient exponent periods, not necessarily the smallest period.

runs.text: . Here gcd(7,40)=1 and phi(40)=16, so reduce 222 to 14 modulo 16.

items.text: Do not use Fermat's theorem with a composite modulus merely because the exponent resembles n-1.
Do not infer primality from a single successful Fermat congruence; composite pseudoprimes exist.
A zero reduced exponent represents a full period, not necessarily the literal exponent zero in an uncoprime setting.
